Bundle sheath cells in C4 plants are characterised by a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange, and no intercellular spaces.

In C4 plants, the primary CO2 acceptor is the 3-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), located in the mesophyll cells, and the enzyme responsible for this fixation is PEP carboxylase (PEPcase); mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO.

ku_facts: RuBisCO is described as the most abundant enzyme in the world and its active site can bind to both CO2 and O2, which is reflected in its name.
RuBisCO has a much greater affinity for CO2 when the CO2:O2 ratio is nearly equal, and the binding of CO2 and O2 to RuBisCO is competitive.

In C3 plants, some O2 binds to RuBisCO, causing RuBP to combine with O2 instead of CO2, forming one molecule of phosphoglycerate and one molecule of phosphoglycolate (a 2-carbon compound) in a pathway called photorespiration.
In the photorespiratory pathway, there is no synthesis of sugars, no synthesis of ATP, and no synthesis of NADPH; instead, CO2 is released with the utilisation of ATP.
The biological function of photorespiration is not yet known.

In C4 plants, photorespiration does not occur because they have a mechanism that increases the concentration of CO2 at the enzyme site, achieved when C4 acid from the mesophyll is broken down in bundle sheath cells to release CO2.
The increased intracellular CO2 concentration in C4 plants ensures that RuBisCO functions primarily as a carboxylase, minimising its oxygenase activity.
The absence of photorespiration in C4 plants is associated with better productivity, higher yields, and tolerance to higher temperatures compared to C3 plants.
questions.ku_summary: Photorespiration occurs in C3 plants when O2 competes with CO2 for binding at the active site of RuBisCO, causing RuBP to react with O2 to produce phosphoglycolate in a pathway that consumes ATP and releases CO2 without producing sugars, ATP, or NADPH. C4 plants avoid photorespiration by concentrating CO2 at the RuBisCO site through breakdown of C4 acids in bundle sheath cells, thereby suppressing RuBisCO's oxygenase activity and enabling greater productivity and heat tolerance. The biological function of photorespiration remains unknown.

options.A: C4 plants fix CO2 only in mesophyll cells, completely bypassing RuBisCO and its dual affinity for O2
options.B: C4 plants break down C4 acids in bundle sheath cells to release CO2, raising the CO2 concentration at the RuBisCO site so that its carboxylase activity dominates over its oxygenase activity, preventing photorespiration
options.C: C4 plants possess a modified form of RuBisCO that has no affinity for O2, so photorespiration cannot occur regardless of O2 levels

questions.explanation: In C4 plants, C4 acids formed in mesophyll cells are transported to bundle sheath cells where they are broken down to release CO2. As a result, photorespiration is suppressed, and unlike the C3 photorespiratory pathway (which consumes ATP and releases CO2 without producing sugars or NADPH), carbon is efficiently fixed into sugars — contributing to better productivity, higher yields, and tolerance to higher temperatures in C4 plants.

ku_facts: The average velocity of all free electrons in a conductor is zero in the absence of an electric field because their directions after collisions are completely random.
When an electric field E is present, each electron is accelerated with acceleration a = –eE/m, where –e is the charge and m is the mass of an electron.
The velocity of the ith electron at time t is Vi = vi + (–eE/m)ti, where vi is its velocity immediately after its last collision and ti is the time elapsed since that last collision.
The average time between successive collisions is called the relaxation time, denoted τ, and the average value of ti over all electrons equals τ.
The drift velocity vd is defined as the average velocity of all electrons and is given by vd = –(eτ/m)E, which is independent of time even though electrons are being accelerated.
The magnitude of current is related to drift speed by I = neA|vd|, where n is the number of free electrons per unit volume, e is the electron charge, and A is the cross-sectional area.
The current density j is related to the electric field E by j = (ne²τ/m)E, which reproduces Ohm's law with conductivity σ = ne²τ/m.

Resistivity depends inversely on both the number n of free electrons per unit volume and the average time t between collisions, as expressed by r = m / (n e^2 t).

ku_facts: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule states that at any junction, the sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to the sum of currents leaving the junction.
The Junction Rule is justified by the fact that when currents are steady, there is no accumulation of charges at any junction or at any point in a line.
Kirchhoff's Loop Rule states that the algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells in the loop is zero.
The Loop Rule is justified because electric potential is dependent on location, so returning to the same starting point in a closed loop means the total change in potential must be zero.
For a cell with current I flowing from negative terminal N to positive terminal P, the potential difference between terminals is V = V(P) – V(N) = e – Ir.
If the current I through a cell is labelled as flowing from positive terminal P to negative terminal N, then the potential difference is V = e + Ir.
If a determined current value is positive, the actual current flows in the direction of the arrow assigned during labelling; if negative, the current flows opposite to that arrow.
The series and parallel combination formulae for resistors are not always sufficient to determine all currents and potential differences in a circuit, which is why Kirchhoff's rules are needed.
questions.ku_summary: Kirchhoff's two rules provide a systematic method for analysing electric circuits that cannot be reduced by simple series and parallel formulae. The Junction Rule requires current conservation at every node (no charge accumulation under steady conditions), while the Loop Rule requires that the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop equals zero (since potential is single-valued). Together, these rules allow all unknown currents and potential differences in an arbitrarily complex network to be determined.
